turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, what brings me in is that I just... I feel like I can’t settle in my own body anymore. It's really bad, especially when I’m supposed to sit quietly and handle paperwork or, like, figure out shared household plans with my husband. Which, honestly, he's been so stressed lately because of his new manager at work. The guy used to run a whole different department and now he expects everyone to just pivot overnight, and it's causing all this tension. My husband comes home and just vents for hours, and I try to listen, but I’m just sitting there feeling this... this buzzing in my arms and legs, you know? Like I need to get up and rearrange the entire living room right that second instead of just sitting there. But yeah, the paperwork and the sitting still... it's just getting impossible.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes feeling unable to settle in her own body, experiencing a 'buzzing' in her arms and legs, and finding it impossible to sit still.

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to your childhood and school years, were you always someone who had trouble sitting still and staying focused, or is this restless feeling something that's more new for you in recent years?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, looking back... no, it's definitely not new. It was already a huge part of me in elementary school. I was always that girl with the incredibly messy desk. Like, papers shoved everywhere, half-eaten snacks, broken crayons. And the forgotten permission slips! Oh my gosh, actually, speaking of permission slips, I remember this one time in fourth grade, we were supposed to go to the state aquarium, and of course, I forgot my slip. My mom had to drive all the way down to the school to sign it in person, and she was driving this awful old station wagon back then—it was this hideous pea-green color, and the AC was completely busted, so she was so sweaty and mad when she got to the front office. She hated that car so much. We ended up selling it to my uncle a few years later, and he tried to fix it up but eventually just scrapped it for parts because the transmission blew. 

But um, anyway, what was I... right, school. Yeah, my mom got a lot of notes. The teachers were always writing home about me, saying I talked out of turn constantly or that I just seemed completely unable to stay seated during lessons. So, yeah, I guess it's been there pretty much forever.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient agrees with the doctor's premise that she has had trouble staying focused since elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes having an incredibly messy desk with papers and items shoved everywhere.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going off on a tangent about her mother's car and losing her original train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient recalls frequently forgetting her permission slips for school.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions that teachers frequently wrote notes saying she was completely unable to stay seated during lessons.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about having a restless feeling, stating it has been a huge part of her since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient notes that teachers complained she talked out of turn constantly.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting there feeling that buzzing in your arms and legs and needing to get up, is there usually a lot of worry or anxiety running through your mind at the same time, or is it more just a physical restlessness without the worry?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really worry. It’s not like my brain is spinning with bad thoughts or panicking or anything. It’s really just my body. Like my muscles are just... awake? It actually reminds me of when my husband and I tried to go see that three-hour historical drama last weekend. Oh my gosh, the costumes were incredible, but the seats in that theater were just terrible. They were those faux-leather recliners, which sounds nice, right? But they squeaked every single time you shifted your weight. And the guy next to us had this giant tub of popcorn and he was chewing with his mouth wide open. I swear, people have zero theater etiquette anymore. 

Like, back when I was getting my bachelor's degree, we used to go to this little indie theater downtown, and if you even whispered, the owner would come down the aisle with a flashlight and literally shush you. He was this grumpy older guy named Arthur who always wore these ridiculous bright red suspenders and he took the movies so seriously. The place eventually closed down to make way for a coffee shop, which was a shame because... wait, what were you asking? 

Oh, right, the buzzing. Yeah, no, I'm not really anxious or worrying when it happens. It's just a physical thing.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by her own unrelated thoughts about a movie theater and loses track of the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms experiencing physical restlessness, describing her body and muscles as feeling 'awake' without accompanying anxiety.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about movie theaters, seats, and past experiences.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies that her physical restlessness is accompanied by worry, anxiety, or panicking thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on tasks like that paperwork or planning with your husband, do you find it hard to organize your thoughts, get started, or finish what you begin—or is it mainly just the physical restlessness that's the problem?
turns.patient_response:
Um, yeah, it's definitely not just the physical part. Getting things done is... it's a whole ordeal. Like, if my husband asks me to handle a few things in order—say, call the plumber, update the shared calendar, and send off some form—I’ll usually manage to do the first part. I'll call the plumber. But then, while I'm on the phone, I'll notice a stain on the kitchen counter, and I'll start scrubbing that. Which reminds me, we really need to switch to a different countertop cleaner because the lemon one we have right now smells so artificial, kind of like those cheap hard candies they give out at banks? I used to love going to the bank with my dad when I was little just for those candies. He knew the teller, Brenda, and she always gave me two. She had this massive hair, like, straight out of the 80s, even though it was the 90s, and she wore these huge plastic earrings that clacked against the phone when she talked. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll start scrubbing the counter, and then I'll completely drift into something else, and before I know it, the calendar isn't updated and the form is just sitting there. I just... I can't seem to follow through on the whole list before my brain just goes somewhere else.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they fail to finish a list of tasks given by their husband, leaving things like updating the calendar and sending forms undone.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as noticing a stain on the counter while on the phone, which derails their current task.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, drifting from countertop cleaner to bank candies, childhood memories, and a bank teller's appearance before returning to the topic.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned these issues go back to elementary school. But I want to make sure I have the timeline right: were you having trouble with focus, organization, and following through on tasks consistently throughout your entire childhood and teenage years, or did things get noticeably worse at some point?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it was always there, like I said about school and the messy desk. But honestly, it got noticeably worse a lot more recently. Specifically, since I got married and our routines merged, which was about a year and five months ago. 

Merging two lives is... wow. He moved into my place, and he brought all these heavy boxes of vintage vinyl records. Which, I mean, I love music, but he insists on keeping them perfectly alphabetized, and then he bought this massive mid-century modern record console that takes up half the living room. We had to move my grandmother's armchair into the guest room just to make it fit, and the guest room is already full of my craft supplies that I never use. I bought all this yarn a few years ago thinking I was going to knit sweaters for everyone for Christmas, but I only ever finished half a scarf. It’s this chunky mustard yellow yarn, actually really itchy, so maybe it's a good thing I stopped. I should probably just donate it. There’s a Goodwill right next to that bakery we love... 

Wait. What were we talking about? 

Oh! Right, if things got worse. Yeah, so it was always an issue when I was younger, but it’s been so much more obvious and harder to keep a handle on since we got married and had to actually combine our daily routines a year and five months ago.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms the doctor's premise that they have had trouble with focus consistently since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient confirms a history of trouble following through on tasks and gives an example of starting to knit sweaters but only finishing half a scarf.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms long-standing organization issues, referencing a 'messy desk' and finding it hard to keep a handle on their combined routines.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts during the response, going on a long tangent about records, yarn, and a bakery before forgetting the question.

turns.doctor_question: Before you got married, when you were living alone, were you able to manage tasks like paying bills, keeping your space organized, or completing projects on your own—or were those things just as difficult back then?
turns.patient_response:
Um, it was still pretty difficult back then, honestly. Like, I'd keep meaning to return phone calls or pay a bill, and then days would just pass without me doing it. Or I’d be supposed to bring something to a meeting, and I wouldn't even remember until I was already in the car. 

Oh my gosh, my old car back then was this tiny silver hatchback, and the air conditioning was totally broken. In the summer, it was just brutal. I had to drive everywhere with the windows rolled all the way down, which meant my hair was always a complete disaster by the time I got anywhere. I used to go to this amazing little salon right down the street from my apartment to try and manage the frizz. The stylist there, Gina, she had this little French Bulldog that would literally sit on your lap while you were waiting for your color to process. He snored so loudly! I always wanted a dog, but my building had a super strict no-pets policy. The landlord, Mr. Henderson, was so particular about the rules—he actually threatened to fine me once because I left my umbrella out in the hallway to dry. It was one of those clear bubble umbrellas? I loved that thing, it made me feel like I was in a movie when it rained. 

But anyway... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, living alone. Yeah, I was definitely still forgetting to pay bills and bring things with me even before my husband moved in. It just felt a little less obvious because there was no one else around to notice it.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about her car, a salon, a dog, and an umbrella before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly confirms forgetting daily activities, such as returning phone calls, paying bills, and bringing necessary items to meetings.
